newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - February 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - February 14.

text.p: The following are the highlights of stories reported in the Irish press on Friday.
- Senior loyalists said on Thursday night they were "cautiously optimistic" their ceasefire would hold, adding that President Clinton's appeal for restraint "certainly would carry weight".

- A serious problem has arisen in the senior management ranks of Radio Ireland with the chief executive Dan Collins under pressure to relinquish his post only a few weeks before the new station comes on air.
- Irish potato growers are considering dumping upwards of 30,000 tonnes because oversupply in the market has sent prices plummeting, it emerged on Thursday.
- The Irish stock market has reached a notable landmark with the ISEQ Overall Index soaring through the 3,000 barrier amid strong demand for all the leading and industrial stocks.
- A high-powered delegation from the National Treasuries Management Agency has been successful in persuading the international rating agency Moody's not to downgrade Ireland's domestic debt.
- Family doctors who prescribe contraception to young teens have been told they must not tell parents without the girls' consent.
- The leaders of the country's biggest nursing union made a coded appeal on Thursday for support for the new 80 million Irish pound deal.
- Ireland's Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn is preparing to bring to the Irish cabinet an independent study of top peoples' pay.
- Rapidly rising house prices risk fuelling inflation and could threaten Ireland's fitness to join the European single currency, an EU report warned.
- Ireland's top doctors could be put out of business by new hikes in insurance costs which bring their payments to more than seven million Irish pounds this year.
- The Irish government on Thursday night seriously cautioned Irish hauliers to delay journeys to Spain because of the dangers posed by the worsening blockades there.
- The serious crime rate in Ireland has fallen for the first time since 1989, Minister for Justice Nora Owen said on Thursday.
- Ireland's economic performance last year was second only to its performance in 1995 in terms of new companies being established, a new company survey has revealed.
- Ireland's Social Welfare Minister Proinsias de Rossa on Thursday launched the first stage of a review of the pensions market in the country.
